claims.statement: Slow-deactivating inward current (activated by depolarisation, deactivated by hyperpolarisation, time constant ~200-300ms)
predicts: After hyperpolarisation, rebound firing is suppressed because the inward current is deactivated
More negative hyperpolarisation causes more suppression (dose-response)
Brief depolarisation before test boosts firing (current reactivates)
Paired pulses show facilitation because first pulse activates current, second benefits
claims.conflicts: H1 and H2 both explain the depol/hyperpol asymmetry but differ on kinetics — H1 has slow deactivation (hundreds of ms), H2 has slow Na recovery (also slow but different voltage dependence)
claims.note: Observed spike_count=13.5 after hyperpolarising conditioning matches H1 prediction [12,18]. Data confirms slow-deactivating inward current hypothesis.

claims.statement: Slow Na inactivation/recovery (slow_na=true) — Na channels recover slowly from inactivation at hyperpolarised potentials
predicts: After hyperpolarisation, Na channels recover slowly → fewer spikes in test
More negative hyperpolarisation accelerates recovery → more spikes (opposite to H1!)
Paired pulses show reduced second response due to Na inactivation
claims.conflicts: H2 differs from H1 in that the mechanism is slow Na recovery rather than an explicit extra current; both predict similar conditioning effects but H2 predicts stronger frequency-dependent adaptation
claims.note: P8 probe measured 13.5 spikes, which is outside H2's predicted band [0,8]. The observation falls in the kill band [13,15] for H2. H2 (slow Na recovery) is refuted.

claims.statement: Both slow-deactivating inward current AND slow Na recovery contribute to rebound behavior
predicts: Combines predictions of H1 and H2
Both mechanisms contribute to the observed patterns
More complex model but better fit
claims.conflicts: H3 combines H1 and H2; if supported, it explains all observations but is less parsimonious
claims.note: P8 probe measured 13.5 spikes, which falls in H3's support band [12, 18]. However, H3 claims a combined mechanism including both slow-deactivating inward current AND slow Na recovery. Since H2 (slow Na recovery) was just refuted by the same probe (13.5 outside H2's [0,8] band), H3's combined mechanism is incorrect. H3 is refuted because it includes a wrong component.

attacks.text: H2 (slow Na recovery) predicted spike_count ∈ [0,8] after hyperpolarising conditioning, but P3 probe measured 13.5. The gap of 5.5 spikes (with reps=2 averaged) cannot be explained by variance. H2's core mechanism - that slow Na channel recovery reduces firing - contradicts the data. The observed 13.5 spikes aligns with H1's prediction [12,18] of a slow-deactivating inward current. H2 is refuted by this probe.

H3 claims both slow-deactivating inward current AND slow Na recovery contribute. P3 probe refuted H2's slow Na recovery component (predicted [0,8], observed 13.5). Since one of H3's two proposed mechanisms is incorrect, H3's combined model is not supported. H1 alone explains the data without requiring the additional slow Na component.

H1 SUPPORTED by P3/P8 probes (13.5 spikes in [12,18]), but the hypothesis ignores several constraints: (1) The 'slow-deactivating inward current' is not identified — could be HCN, persistent Na, or T-type Ca2+; the campaign only characterized kinetics, not molecular identity. (2) The forecast for held-out protocols assumed linear voltage-dependence of deactivation, but real currents may have non-monotonic I-V relationships. (3) Campaign only tested seed 0 of ca_rebound world; kinetics may vary across seeds. (4) No voltage-clamp data to directly measure the current's reversal potential or conductance. (5) The 40-spike response after depolarizing conditioning may saturate — H1 predicts enhancement but not ceiling effects. These are scope constraints, not refutations.
